The proposed new cooling designs used tangentially injected coolant from one pass to the second pass through holes in the divider wall to generate swirling flow.
The spanwise-averaged Nusselt number ratios on the walls increased with increasing Reynolds number from 10,000 to 50,000.
The double row configuration of holes in the divider wall created two counter-rotating swirls to enhance heat transfer on both walls equally.
The new swirl-generating designs showed higher thermal performance parameters compared to rib turbulator studies.

The study examined the assumption of neglecting the effects of channel taper from hub to tip, and found that the local straight, two-pass channel data can be used to represent the typically tapered internal coolant channels.
The new designs eliminated the need for complex rib turbulators, which are difficult to manufacture, and produced significantly higher heat transfer enhancements with lower pressure drops.
The detailed local heat transfer coefficient data was presented for the proposed new cooling designs and the straight and tapered channels with and without ribs.
Flow visualization using smoke was conducted to understand the flow patterns inside the two-pass channels.
The new cooling designs have the potential to resist the centrifugal and Coriolis forces generated by the rotating turbine blades.
The study focused on improving the internal cooling of turbine blades to enable higher turbine inlet temperatures and engine performance.
The progress in developing new materials to withstand the high temperatures in modern gas turbines is not keeping pace with the increase in engine temperatures.
Effective internal cooling is the best way to cool turbine blades as it affects the mainstream flow the least compared to external cooling techniques.
